analysis.title: CIO View: Listed real estate
key_insights: UBS CIO favors listed real estate companies that pursue growth, acquire through accretive issuance, and show strong pricing power, profitable pipelines, attractive yield gaps and robust cash flows. It stays selective on companies trading at a discount to NAV, which may be value traps unless they grow.

UBS expects overall real estate values to keep appreciating over the medium term with further rental growth. In the short term, higher interest costs and opportunity costs may weigh on secondary property valuations. Earnings yields relative to equities are mildly attractive.

Regional preferences: attractive are Hong Kong, Japanese and Singapore developers, the UK and the US. Unattractive are Australia, Continental Europe, Hong Kong REITs, Japanese REITs and Singapore REITs, relative to the FTSE EPRA/Nareit Developed Total Return Index in local currencies.

UK is favored as relatively inexpensive because interest rates have already risen significantly. Continental Europe looks cheap and inflation uncertainty should diminish in coming months, but expectations of significantly higher energy prices keep uncertainty high.
In Asia, UBS prefers developers over REITs because REITs show weak momentum in a rising rate environment. It keeps its preference for US REITs despite recent volatility, citing solid fundamentals.

In Australia, a peak in interest rates and lower financing cost pressure have improved prospects, though uncertainty remains high. UBS stays cautious on Japanese REITs because of volatile bond market conditions, though market fundamentals are robust.

Market review: listed real estate outperformed equities early in 2026 on defensive traits, rate cut expectations and solid fundamentals, then volatility returned as long-term US bonds sold off. Higher government bond yields and geopolitical tension raised risk premiums, and the year is repeating 2025's pattern of underperformance while tech and AI firms attract capital.

Global direct real estate transaction volumes rose about 15% y/y last year and UBS expects similar growth in 2026 after a strong start. First-half volumes were encouraging and resilient. Trade uncertainty and corporate indecision have receded, and tariffs are no longer a significant headwind for industrial real estate, given the data center boom.

UBS expects real estate stocks to stay volatile, with potential to bounce back once inflation peaks. A steeper US yield curve is not necessarily negative and depends on whether it reflects stronger growth or tighter liquidity. The earlier curve inversion was a key factor in the sector's underperformance versus global equities.

UBS thinks investors may be underestimating supply constraints across real estate markets. Exceptions are US Sun Belt residential, the US West Coast office market and the Hong Kong office market, though conditions there are improving. Office take-up and retail demand have improved but not reached new highs, and rental income growth is offsetting slightly higher financing costs.
Global listed real estate trades at a discount to NAV of about 12% as of 19 October 2026. Health care, lodging, retail and self storage are outperforming, while residential and office lag.

UBS expects listed real estate EPS growth of 11% in 2026 and 7.7% in 2027 (excluding emerging markets), driven by rental indexation, reversion and select transactions or acquisitions. Most companies should keep financing costs stable or offset increases with rental income, and average debt maturities exceed five years in most markets.

Global average dividend yield is 3.5% versus a seven-year average of 3.6% (excluding EM). REITs trade at about a 3% discount to NAV per UBS estimates. The 12-month forward P/E is at its long-term average of 14-15x. UBS expects a medium-term rerating, delayed again by bond yield volatility.

Index forecasts for the FTSE EPRA/Nareit Developed Index: 6,729 on 21 Oct 26, then 7,200 by Dec 26, 8,000 by Mar 27, 8,400 by Jun 27 and 8,600 by Sep 27. Upside scenario June 2027 target is 8,800 and downside scenario is 8,000.

sector_views.rationale: Earnings growth of 11% in 2026, a roughly 12% discount to NAV, mildly attractive earnings yields versus equities and an expected medium-term rerating.

sector_views.sector: Health care, lodging, retail, self storage real estate

sector_views.rationale: Both subsectors are lagging, though UBS notes conditions in US Sun Belt residential, US West Coast office and Hong Kong office are improving.

earnings_insights: UBS forecasts listed real estate EPS growth of 11% in 2026 and 7.7% in 2027, excluding emerging markets, estimate not reported figures, driven by rental indexation, reversion and select portfolio transactions or acquisitions.

macro_indicators.indicator: Global direct real estate transaction volumes
macro_indicators.reading: about +15% y/y in 2025, similar growth expected in 2026
macro_indicators.interpretation: Resilient transaction volumes support property values and signal stable activity despite bond market volatility.

macro_indicators.indicator: Global listed real estate dividend yield
macro_indicators.interpretation: Yield is slightly below its historical average, consistent with a modest valuation premium to history.

risk_factors: Higher government bond yields raise opportunity costs and slow repricing momentum.
Companies at a discount to NAV may be value traps unless they grow.
Higher interest costs may weigh on secondary property valuations in the short term.

Downside scenario: high cap rates, weak rental reversion, tenant incentives and stagnating occupancy prevent property values from rising, and the retail/office versus logistics dislocation fails to revert.
Open-ended funds facing redemptions are likely to sell properties.
Energy price uncertainty in Continental Europe and volatile bond markets in Japan.
vol_and_positioning: Listed real estate is expected to remain volatile, with potential to bounce back once inflation peaks.
Long-term US bond market sell-off and volatility in government bond yields are the main source of sector volatility, and prolonged bond volatility may keep corporate investment decisions on hold.
geopolitical: Ongoing geopolitical tensions have raised risk premiums in listed real estate.
Changing expectations of significantly higher energy prices create uncertainty for Continental Europe.
Trade uncertainty has receded and tariffs are no longer a significant headwind for industrial real estate.

tension_points.bull_case: Rental growth, 11% EPS growth in 2026, a 12% discount to NAV and mildly attractive earnings yields support a medium-term rerating toward an 8,400 index level by June 2027.
tension_points.bear_case: High bond yields keep risk premiums and cap rates elevated, rental growth slows and weak reversions leave property values flat, giving an 8,000 downside target.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Persistent high long-end rates with weak rental reversions, tenant incentives and stagnating occupancy.

theme_stances.key_argument: Earnings growth and a discount to NAV support a medium-term rerating that bond yield volatility has delayed.
theme_stances.evidence: We are optimistic at the index level, expecting a rerating over the medium term

theme_stances.key_argument: In Asia, developers are preferred because REITs show weak momentum in a rising interest rate environment.
theme_stances.evidence: we prefer developers over REITs, as the latter exhibit weak momentum
